summary:
SPHEREx Sky Change is a free, public web tool for watching the sky evolve in SPHEREx data. By entering a sky coordinate (RA/Dec) or object name, users can play every SPHEREx image of that region chronologically like a short video, making moving or variable objects easy to spot.

Within the player, users can add or subtract images taken months apart, or stack all six detectors for a cleaner view. Clicking any point generates its spectrum and light curve on the fly. The platform also lets users overlay Gaia DR3 and CatWISE catalogs, inspect contamination flags, and share or embed views via URL, while automatically ingesting new SPHEREx data releases.

Validated on all five challenge targets, the tool measured Barnard's Star moving 10.07″ in 361 days (closely matching the 10.30″ catalog prediction) and independently identified the variable stars R Draconis and RW Aurigae.

Because SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months across 102 bands, the dataset is far too vast for professionals to inspect manually. Opening visual inspection to the public accelerates the discovery of nearby brown dwarfs, asteroids, and other dynamic celestial objects.

1. The Challenge and Our Approach

1.1 The Problem

Many of the most significant discoveries in the solar neighborhood were made by comparing images of the same patch of sky taken at different epochs. Pluto was discovered this way in 1930, and citizen scientists in the Backyard Worlds project have identified hundreds of brown dwarfs by visually blinking multi-epoch WISE images. Launched in 2025, NASA's SPHEREx mission provides an unprecedented all-sky dataset for time-domain infrared astronomy, mapping the entire sky twice a year across 102 spectral bands from 0.75 to 5.0 µm. The challenge calls for an open, browser-based tool that allows anyone to enter a sky position, view chronological SPHEREx imagery as a smooth time-lapse so moving objects stand out, and validate performance on five benchmark targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

However, SPHEREx data present substantial instrumental challenges compared to conventional broadband blink surveys. Each detector carries a linear variable filter (LVF), meaning the observed wavelength varies spatially across the focal plane and consecutive exposures of the same star sample different wavelengths. In addition, the point-spread function (PSF) is undersampled (with a full width at half maximum of ≈5″ on 6.15″ pixels), bright stars saturate, and observations are distributed across evolving data releases (QR2, QR3, and DR1) that supersede earlier reductions. A naive viewer that ignores these instrumental properties will falsely depict a steady star as "changing" simply because its sampled wavelength shifted between exposures.

1.2 Research Questions and Key Benchmarks

Our system design addresses four core questions:

  • Q1. Accessibility and Latency: Can any user—armed only with a web browser and a sky coordinate—stream chronological SPHEREx imagery of an arbitrary field within roughly one minute?
  • Q2. Quantitative Science: Can the platform move beyond visual inspection to measure proper motions, extract spectra, and quantify variability with calibrated uncertainties and catalog cross-matches?
  • Q3. Blind Automated Discovery: Can automated pipelines detect moving and variable sources blindly without prior catalog seeding, and how accurately do they perform on known ground-truth objects?
  • Q4. Responsible Public Participation: Can citizen scientists meaningfully contribute by vetting candidates and querying an AI assistant without mistaking unconfirmed candidates for verified discoveries?

All five challenge targets are validated on the live platform, and our automated pipelines recover all three fast-moving objects and both variable stars blindly. Every metric reported in this document is reproduced directly from the repository's validation artifacts and live pages, including null results and current limitations. .

1.4 Core Methodology Overview

Rather than treating SPHEREx's spatially varying wavelength as nuisance noise, we model it directly as physical signal. Every exposure is reprojected onto a common tangent-plane sky grid alongside its own per-pixel wavelength map. For any pixel, a local reference image is constructed exclusively from exposures acquired by the same detector within 3% of the target wavelength, ensuring that difference images highlight genuine astrophysical motion or variability rather than color gradients. Clicking any pixel samples one wavelength measurement from each of hundreds of overlapping exposures, assembling a complete 0.75–5.0 µm spectrum on the fly. Survey passes separated by six months provide the time baseline for stellar proper motions and the Earth-orbit parallax baseline for distant Solar System bodies. External catalogs (Gaia, CatWISE, and JPL) are used strictly for labeling and validation, never for candidate selection.

2.2 Ingestion and Sky-Grid Alignment Pipeline

  1. Archive Discovery: The backend queries IRSA's Simple Image Access (SIA) service across all active SPHEREx collections. A daily query to IRSA's Table Access Protocol (TAP) checks for newly published spherex_qrN and spherex_drN releases, enabling automatic adoption without code modifications. When multiple releases cover the same exposure and detector, the latest reduction takes precedence (DR over QR, ordered by release number).
  2. Cutout Retrieval: To accommodate detector position-angle rotations, cutouts are requested at 1.5× the target field width. Zodiacal light is subtracted (IMAGE - ZODI) alongside corresponding VARIANCE and FLAGS extensions. Per-pixel wavelengths are evaluated from the WAVE-TAB world-coordinate table on an 8-pixel grid and interpolated, while the effective PSF (DR1/QR3) or optical PSF cube (QR2) is resampled onto a 101 ×101 grid at 10× oversampling.
  3. Spatial Reprojection: Science images, variance maps, and wavelength maps are bilinearly resampled—and bitmask flags nearest-neighbor resampled—onto a common tangent-plane grid with 6.15″ pixels. Coverage edges are eroded by 3 pixels, residual sky background is subtracted, and exposures covering less than 5% of the field are discarded.
  4. Epoch-Aware Cataloging: Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 sources are stored in field pixel coordinates together with their reference epochs and annual pixel proper motions, allowing the frontend to propagate every catalog marker to the exact observation date of each pass.

3. Theoretical Foundation and Methods

3.1 Wavelength-Matched Difference Imaging

For an exposure I at a given pixel, we construct a matched reference R as the per-pixel median of exposures from the same detector acquired at least 3 hours earlier or later (ensuring moving objects have shifted away) whose local wavelength lies within 3% of I. Up to 36 closest-wavelength exposures are combined and scaled by a factor α—the median ratio I/R across pixels with reference S/N > 30, clipped to [0.7, 1.4] (typically 0.83–1.13). The difference signal-to-noise ratio is computed as:

S/N = (I − αR) / √(σ_I² + α²σ_R² + (εαR)²), σ_R² = π⟨σ_j²⟩ / (2n)

where ε= 0.1 accounts for bright-star subtraction residuals induced by the undersampled PSF. Crucially, this systematic error term depends solely on the reference flux αR; an earlier formulation using max(I, R) artificially capped bright genuine movers at S/N ≈1/ε= 10. Local peaks with S/N ≥5 advance as moving-object candidates.

Figure 2. End-to-end asteroid detection pipeline. Highlighted stages denote SPHEREx-specific adaptations (wavelength-matched reference construction) and deep-learning real/bogus classification.

3.2 Joint Spectral and Temporal Modeling

Because consecutive exposures sample a source at different wavelengths, raw flux time series entangle intrinsic spectral shape with temporal brightness variations. For automated variable-star detection, we model the flux in detector d as the product of a smooth polynomial spectrum and a pass-dependent brightness scaling factor L_d(p(t)):

F_d(λ, t) = S_d(λ) · L_d(p(t)), ln S_d = Σ (k = 0 … K) c_k (ln λ)^k

The model is fitted directly in linear flux space—avoiding per-point S/N cuts that would bias noisier epochs upward—using iterative sigma clipping and zero-point calibration anchored to ensemble field stars. Candidates require a statistically significant variation in L_d corroborated across at least two detectors. For interactive user queries, sorting exposures by wavelength yields an instantaneous spectrum, while grouping by detector and epoch produces multi-band light curves.

3.3 Earth-Orbit Parallax for Distant Solar System Bodies

An outer Solar System body at heliocentric distance d exhibits apparent sky motion dominated by Earth's orbital parallax, modulated by slow Keplerian drift:

θ(t) = θ₀ + μ(t − t₀) − (1 AU / d) · P⊥(t), |μ| ≤ √2 · ω_circ(d)

where P_⊥(t) denotes Earth's barycentric position projected onto the plane of the sky (in AU) and ω_circ(d) is the circular orbital angular velocity at distance d. Bounding the proper motion |µ| at the local escape velocity breaks the degeneracy between parallactic distance and linear drift. The pipeline searches a logarithmic grid of trial distances from 30 to 3000 AU, linking at most one detection group per survey pass across a minimum of three passes (since any two-epoch offset can be absorbed by linear drift). For sources below single-exposure detection limits, difference frames within each pass are shifted along trial trajectories and co-added (shift-and-stack).

3.4 Blind Proper-Motion Detection and Cross-Epoch Astrometry

In the single-mission proper-motion search, sources are detected and centroided via 2D Gaussian fits in the first and final pass stacks, which are astrometrically registered to the ensemble of field stars. The significance of an apparent displacement Δ is evaluated as:

z = |Δ| / √(σ_fit² + σ_sys²)

where σ_sys is an empirical astrometric noise floor measured on bright field stars. To reject chromatic centroid shifts caused by unresolved color blends, the displacement vector must align consistently across at least two independent detector arrays, the initial position must be vacated, and intermediate passes must fall along the linear trajectory. Only after candidate selection do Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 cross-matches classify detections as known movers, stationary artifacts, or new candidates. A complementary second stage compares SPHEREx epoch positions against CatWISE2020 (≈2015.4), establishing a ≈10.5-year baseline capable of resolving much slower proper motions.

3.5 Probability Calibration

Raw logits z produced by the real/bogus neural network are calibrated into posterior probabilities via temperature scaling fitted on held-out validation fields, with the detection threshold fixed at a 1% false-positive rate:

p = 1 / (1 + e^(−z/T)), T = 0.780, p_threshold ≈ 0.597

3.6 Multi-Criteria Point-Source Diagnostics ("Is It a Star?")

Clicking any source in the Control Room triggers an eight-step diagnostic check: (1) an all-exposure median stack to reject transient artifacts; (2) aperture S/N relative to a local sky annulus; (3) Gaussian width comparison against up to 25 isolated Gaia stars in the field (classifying sources with width ratios > 1.6 as extended and < 0.55 as sharp hot-pixel artifacts); (4) per-exposure detection persistence; (5) quality-flag fractions; (6) epoch-propagated catalog cross-matching; (7) spectral model comparison between a blackbody grid (2300–40,000 K) and a power-law continuum (flagging galaxies when a power law provides a substantially superior fit); and (8) proximity to CNN moving-object detections. Each source receives an automated classification of star, extended, sharp, transient, saturated, unfit, or none.

4.1 Real/Bogus Convolutional Neural Network

  • Architecture: Three convolutional blocks (32, 64, and 128 channels, each comprising two 3 ×3 convolutions with BatchNorm and ReLU, followed by max-pooling 21 →10 →5), global average and max pooling, and a 256 →128 →1 classification head with dropout (0.3).
  • Training Data: Real known asteroids are strictly excluded from training and reserved entirely for testing. Positive examples consist of synthetic moving point sources—spanning both linear asteroid tracks and distant parallactic trajectories—injected into real exposures using each exposure's own 10× oversampled PSF. Negative examples comprise all other S/N ≥5 detections in the training fields (primarily stellar subtraction residuals, optical ghosts, and cosmic rays), capped at 50,000 per field.
  • Field-Level Data Split: Datasets are partitioned strictly by sky field rather than by individual candidate to prevent spatial leakage: test fields (ecl180+00, ecl060+00), validation fields (ecl120+00, ecl315-12), and 15 bright-asteroid benchmark fields reserved solely for evaluation.
  • Optimization: Trained for 30 epochs using AdamW (lr = 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴), a one-cycle learning-rate schedule, random 90° rotations and flips, and positive-weighted binary cross-entropy, followed by post-hoc temperature scaling on the validation set.

4.2 Brown-Dwarf Spectral Classifier

Clicked spectra are aggregated into 16 logarithmically spaced wavelength bins spanning 0.74–5.0 µm, normalized as log₁₀ flux relative to the brightest bin alongside a 16-element binary coverage mask (requiring at least 5 valid bins). The multilayer perceptron (MLP) is trained on 60,000 synthetic spectra: 50% T and Y brown dwarfs (modeled as blackbodies with randomized CH₄, H₂O, and CO absorption depths) and 50% astrophysical contaminants—including main-sequence and reddened stars, M giants and Miras (hard negatives with deep water bands), L dwarfs, dusty young stellar objects, and galaxies—augmented with neighbor blending, Gaussian noise, and missing spectral channels. Inference executes in pure NumPy, eliminating deep-learning runtime overhead on the web server.

5.2 Asteroid Detection on Unseen Fields

Although the real/bogus CNN never trained on real asteroids, across 19 held-out fields it separates 556 detections of known real asteroids from instrumental false positives with an AUROC of 0.987 (95% CI: 0.981–0.992), retaining 90.8% of real detections at a 1.15% false-positive rate. By contrast, difference-image S/N alone achieves an AUROC of just 0.537—scarcely better than random chance—because bright stellar subtraction residuals frequently match real asteroids in raw significance. Injection tests indicate 50% single-exposure completeness at AB 17.3, with the classifier removing negligible genuine signal.

5.3 Distant Solar System Bodies and Planet Nine Search

  • Injection-Recovery Tests: Synthetic outer Solar System bodies at heliocentric distances of 500, 800, 1500, and 3000 AU (AB 15–17) on randomly oriented circular orbits were injected into five fields and searched by jointly fitting parallax and bounded orbital motion (Equation 3). Across fields with three survey passes, 47 of 48 injected bodies were recovered with a median distance error of 0.09%, whereas zero were linked in a two-pass control field by design. (An earlier prototype that omitted orbital motion during both injection and fitting achieved 59/60 recovery; recognizing this circularity, we replaced it with the full orbital-motion benchmark.)
  • Known Dwarf Planets: Applied blindly to real SPHEREx observations, the parallax pipeline accurately recovered the heliocentric distances of two dwarf planets from SPHEREx astrometry alone: Makemake at 52.71 AU (JPL: 52.72 AU, 0.02% error) and Haumea at 49.49 AU (JPL: 49.82 AU, 0.66% error). A third target, Eris (95.5 AU), fell below single-exposure sensitivity and was not detected.
  • Planet Nine Search: We surveyed 32 fields (7.89 deg²) along the predicted orbital track of Planet Nine (Brown & Batygin 2021) and surrounding the 2025 IRAS/AKARI candidate region. Single-exposure searches yielded no distant candidates. Shift-and-stack processing (50% completeness at AB 19.2) linked 63 candidate tracks across three passes; however, randomizing pass epoch labels yielded 55 and 60 tracks, confirming that the 63 linkages are consistent with random background noise. We report a clean null result, publishing upper limits transparently on the site (covering ≈2.3% of Planet Nine's predicted optical brightness distribution).

Figure 9. Planet Nine search summary page showing 32 fields analyzed, 63 shift-and-stack linkages across three passes, and 39 candidates passing preliminary quality filters—consistent with false-alarm expectations under epoch shuffling. The lower panel highlights blind parallax recoveries of Makemake and Haumea alongside the non-detection of Eris.

5.4 High-Proper-Motion Stars

Across nine pre-analyzed benchmark fields, the blind pass-to-pass proper-motion search produced 0 false positives. To evaluate completeness on an unbiased sample, we tested the pipeline on 45 randomly selected Gaia DR3 high-proper-motion stars (9 < G < 16) within 0.15° fields (Table 7), achieving a median astrometric error of 0.397″ (90th percentile: 0.806″), a median measured-to-catalog motion ratio of 1.047, and zero spurious "new" candidates.

In cross-epoch tests on 658 isolated static stars, per-axis proper-motion scatter is 13.8 mas/yr, with 0 false alarms across 1,300 static control stars. Over a one-year SPHEREx baseline alone, a star must move at roughly 0.7″/yr to produce a detectable centroid shift (0.12 px) and is recovered reliably above 2.0″/yr. Incorporating the 10.5-year CatWISE2020 baseline extends sensitivity down to 0.10–0.15″/yr for the ≈50% of stars sufficiently isolated from neighbors. Following IRSA's retirement of QR2 and our rebuild on DR1 + QR3, recovery on the 45 Gaia benchmark stars declined from 25 to 19 while median astrometric error increased from 0.27″ to 0.40″. While the root cause remains under investigation, the platform transparently displays the before-and-after comparison table. No stellar parallaxes are claimed, as static field stars show 70–135 mas scatter under the same fit (Epsilon Indi B yields 183 ±105 mas vs. 271 mas catalog, and an earlier unregistered 304 ±71 mas estimate was formally withdrawn).

5.5 Variable Stars and R Draconis Phase Verification

Searching 927 isolated stars across nine fields yielded 2 variable candidates—both confirmed catalog variables—with 0 false alarms. Out of 194 VSX or Gaia catalog variables falling within these fields, 40 satisfied the isolation criteria and 2 were flagged; the remaining stars vary by less than ≈8% or oscillate on timescales too short to resolve across 3–4 survey passes. For R Draconis, the observed brightness ordering across passes matches the ephemeris phase of AAVSO VSX (P = 246.12 d), and a fitted 246-day sinusoid exhibits peak variability amplitude at the shortest wavelengths, consistent with Mira-type pulsation physics.

5.7 Brown-Dwarf Classifier and Static-Residual Veto

The spectral classifier assigns scores of 1.000 to Epsilon Indi B and 0.999 to WISE 0855-0714. Across 420 normal Gaia field stars, the median score is 0.000 with a 0.5% false-positive rate at a 0.8 threshold (two stars score ≥0.99, meaning high scores flag candidates for human review rather than proving brown-dwarf status). Prior to a pipeline update on November 12, bright-star subtraction residuals were occasionally linked into spurious fast-moving tracks; implementing a stationary-residual veto eliminated false linkages in high-ecliptic-latitude fields (reducing unidentified tracks from 14 →0 in R Draconis, 21 →0 in Epsilon Indi, and 2 →0 in Barnard's Star) while preserving all genuine asteroid tracks in the Cybele field.


6. In-Site AI Assistant

Every page features an Ask button, complemented by an interactive robot guide in the 3D Control Room and direct object queries in the 3D Universe view. All interfaces route to POST /api/ask, streaming grounded answers powered by Meta Llama 3.2 1B Instruct fine-tuned with LoRA. The entire inference stack runs locally on project infrastructure—no user queries are transmitted to external commercial AI APIs, and prompt text is never logged.

6.1 Retrieval-Augmented Generation Workflow

  1. Context-Aware Query Formulation: User questions are prefixed with the active object or field context (e.g., target Barnard's Star: how fast does it move?).
  2. Multilingual Dense Retrieval: Queries are encoded with BGE-M3 (1024-d) and matched via cosine similarity against the literature corpus, retaining up to 5 passages scoring ≥0.53.
  3. Live Telemetry Injection: For active fields or targets, up to 1,500 characters of live site measurements (exposure counts, measured proper motions, known small bodies, and candidate tracks) are injected into the prompt.
  4. Prompt Assembly: A structured system prompt instructs the model to reply in the user's language, cite retrieved passages using [n] notation, and explicitly state when no supporting literature was retrieved, followed by up to 8 turns of conversation history.
  5. Local Streaming Generation: vLLM serves the merged model on an NVIDIA L4 GPU (temperature = 0.3, max 512 tokens).
  6. Deterministic Provenance Labeling: Whenever zero passages exceed the 0.53 similarity threshold, the UI deterministically attaches a "No source: general knowledge" badge regardless of model output.

Server stability is protected via rate limiting (10 requests/minute and 200/day per user, capped at 4 concurrent streams) and a graceful fallback mode that still surfaces retrieved literature passages if the LLM worker is unavailable.

6.2 Literature Corpus and Multilingual Retriever

The retrieval index comprises 76 scientific papers focused strictly on the SPHEREx mission (instrumentation, survey strategy, data pipeline, Solar System science, and cosmology) and substellar/high-proper-motion astronomy (WISE/CatWISE, Backyard Worlds, Y dwarfs, Planet Nine searches, and the five challenge targets). Full text is indexed exclusively for the 23 papers carrying Creative Commons arXiv licenses, while the remaining 53 contribute titles and abstracts, yielding 1,866 passages (150–400 words each) with full bibliographic metadata. Project documentation is deliberately excluded so the assistant cites peer-reviewed literature rather than itself.

6.5 Live Verification and Known Limitations

  • End-to-End Verification: Asking "How many spectral channels does SPHEREx have?" in Traditional Chinese accurately cited mission papers (102 channels spanning 0.75–5 µm). Querying Barnard's Star combined the catalog rate (10.39″/yr) with the live site measurement (10.07″ over 361.1 days across 356 exposures). Queries for WISE 0855-0714 cited three brown-dwarf papers (≈250 K), while out-of-scope prompts (e.g., film recommendations or pancake recipes) properly triggered the "No source: general knowledge" label.

Figure 10. Live AI assistant on the WISE 0855 page answering "Why is a cold brown dwarf like this one easier to see in the infrared?" The response synthesizes a retrieved paper (Skemer et al. 2016, linked under Sources) with the site's live observation that the brown dwarf is nearly undetectable below 3 µm, accompanied by explicit AI provenance notices.

  • Known Limitations: Without retrieved literature context, the 1B-parameter model can occasionally hallucinate details or garble numerical comparisons. All responses are therefore visibly labeled as AI-generated with clickable citations so users can verify claims directly. Cold-start latency after a server restart is ≈12 s while BGE-M3 initializes, after which streaming begins within 1–2 s.

7. System Architecture

Figure 11. System data flow. Public archives (left) feed the processing pipeline (center) to generate per-field products on disk; the FastAPI backend serves pre-computed layers, executes on-demand photometry and AI inference, and powers the interactive browser client.

7.1 Web Server, Worker Pool, and On-Demand Quick Looks

  • Web Server: FastAPI serves the compiled frontend bundle, static field products, and REST/streaming APIs behind nginx and uvicorn, applying immutable caching to hashed assets, revalidation headers to dynamic JSON/HTML, and strict security headers including a hash-verified Content Security Policy (CSP).
  • Parallel Measurement Pool: On-demand NumPy photometry for /point (spectrum and light curve), /probe, and /starcheck executes across an 8-worker process pool reading memory-mapped field cubes (capped at 4 concurrent requests per user and 64 globally). Extracting a full 357-exposure spectrum on Barnard's Star completes in ≈0.5 s.
  • Atomic Full-Field Rebuilds: Full-field analyses run sequentially in a background queue, writing to staging directories and atomically swapping into production only after all validation checks succeed.
  • Isolated Quick-Look Workers: User-triggered Quick Looks execute as transient systemd units (memory-capped at 6 GB), decoupling them from web-server restarts. Parallel cutout downloads (20 concurrent threads, achieving 1.33 cutouts/s) processed a 0.15° Quick Look of Wolf 359 (254 of 290 exposures downloaded) in roughly four minutes.
  • Automated Maintenance: A weekly systemd timer polls IRSA for newly released exposures and schedules field refreshes whenever sufficient disk headroom is verified via the /health endpoint.
  • Production Deployment: Hosted on a single Google Cloud g2-standard-8 VM in Tokyo equipped with an NVIDIA L4 GPU (dedicated to AI inference) and CPU workers handling image processing and web serving.

8. User Interface and Public Participation

8.1 Search and Streaming Quick Look

The search bar is prominently placed on the landing screen and persistent top navigation bar, accepting decimal or sexagesimal coordinates as well as astronomical object names. Object names are resolved via SIMBAD and propagated using proper motions to the current epoch—an essential step for fast-moving nearby stars such as Barnard's Star, which has shifted by ≈4.6′ since J2000. Pressing Enter initiates a streaming Quick Look: playback starts as soon as the initial frames arrive, stepping through a single detector first for visual steadiness before progressively populating wavelength-matched difference frames and per-pass stacks. Once complete, the field transitions seamlessly into the full interactive Field Lab.

Figure 12. Streaming Quick Look of Wolf 359 (0.15° field), generated on demand without pre-computation. Left: time-lapse player at 1.72 µm on 2025-05-01. Right: temporal and spectral coverage timeline (254 of 290 exposures retrieved) paired with automated proper-motion results.

8.2 Interactive Field Lab

The Field Lab provides five visualization modes (Blink, Single Pass, Add All, Subtract, and Shift-and-Stack), a detector selector (all six combined or individual D1–D6 bandpasses), false-color RGB compositing, zoom controls, contrast/brightness sliders, and toggleable overlays for Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, quality flags, and measured motion vectors. Clicking any pixel plots its 0.75–5.0 µm spectrum and per-detector light curves (Figure 5) with one-click CSV export and an automated brown-dwarf classification score. Dedicated tabs organize target diagnostics, automated moving/variable candidates, external multi-wavelength surveys (Aladin Lite with WISE, 2MASS, DSS2, and SPHEREx HiPS layers), and shareable URL / iframe embed snippets.

8.3 Community Review Queue and Practice Mode

The "Find Movers" review queue presents every candidate identified by the automated pipelines, blinking between the earliest and latest survey passes alongside SPHEREx and catalog motion vectors so visitors can classify candidates as Real, Artifact, or Not Sure. Known catalog movers double as an interactive Practice Mode: ground-truth labels remain concealed until the user casts a vote, training newcomers to distinguish genuine proper motion from PSF residuals before evaluating unconfirmed candidates. Within any Field Lab, visitors can also flag noteworthy positions (moving, variable, unusual spectrum, or other) to publish them to the community queue, and user-flagged Quick Looks are permanently retained.

Figure 13. Public candidate review queue. Each candidate blinks between first and last survey passes with measured and catalog motion vectors overlaid. Top right: empirical recovery completeness curve calibrated on random Gaia high-proper-motion stars.

8.4 3D Universe Explorer, Control Room, and Supporting Views

  • Multi-Scale 3D Explorer: Users can scroll or pinch seamlessly from a procedural Milky Way (70,000 stars) into the Solar System with an interactive epoch scrubber, down to Earth (NASA Blue Marble) showing SPHEREx in its dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit and daily scan ring, and finally onto the SPHEREx all-sky map, where zooming into highlighted regions opens the corresponding Field Lab.
  • 3D Control Room: Clicking the orbiting spacecraft enters an interactive virtual control room whose viewport displays real per-pass stacks, complete with a timeline lever, detector-band color mixers, and click-to-inspect stellar diagnostics (Section 3.6). Clear disclaimers note that SPHEREx is an uncrewed spacecraft and that NASA's WIRE 3D model serves as a visual stand-in.
  • Additional Views: Includes an interactive all-sky map of analyzed fields and targets, a dedicated "Follow an Asteroid or Comet" tracker (powered by IRSA MOST), a NEOSSat coverage tool, the Planet Nine search dashboard, an illustrated User & Validation Guide, a bilingual research paper, and full data attributions.

Figure 14. Interactive all-sky map rendered over the SPHEREx DR1 false-color mosaic, plotting challenge targets, pre-analyzed fields, the simulated Planet X benchmark field, user Quick Looks, the ecliptic plane, and the predicted Planet Nine search band (Brown & Batygin 2021).

8.5 Accessibility, Localization, and Cross-Device Resilience

The entire user interface is localized in English and Traditional Chinese, enforced by automated build tests that fail if any UI string lacks a translation pair. All time-lapse players support full keyboard navigation (Space and arrow keys), the Field Lab supports keyboard pixel selection, auto-play animations respect prefers-reduced-motion, and mobile viewports provide full-width touch and pinch-zoom controls. Devices with low-power GPUs automatically fall back to a lightweight 3D rendering path, backed by a black-frame watchdog and full non-3D fallbacks across every panel.

10. Benefits and Intended Impact

10.1 Target Audiences and Direct Benefits

  • Students and the General Public: Explore dynamic infrared SPHEREx observations immediately in any browser without specialized software or archive expertise, supported by a bilingual AI assistant that explains astronomical phenomena in plain language.
  • Educators and Science Communicators: Share direct deep-linked coordinates or embed live interactive time-lapses inside online lessons, articles, and outreach pages.
  • Professional Researchers: Access rapid visual triage alongside quantitative diagnostics—including per-detector stacks, wavelength-matched difference frames, CSV-exportable spectra and light curves, quality flags, and epoch-propagated catalog overlays.
  • Citizen Scientists: Participate in structured candidate vetting through a review queue that teaches visual classification skills via practice examples before soliciting votes on unconfirmed candidates.

10.2 Broader Scientific and Educational Impact

Because SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months across 102 spectral bands, the resulting multi-epoch dataset is far too vast for manual inspection by professional teams alone. SPHEREx Sky Change democratizes visual and quantitative discovery on this new dataset, enabling anyone with a browser to search for nearby brown dwarfs, main-belt and near-Earth asteroids, high-proper-motion stars, and variable stars. Furthermore, because the backend automatically ingests new IRSA releases, the platform grows more powerful with every six-month sky pass—extending proper-motion baselines for slow stars and adding parallactic epochs for outer Solar System searches.

Equally central to our intended impact is scientific transparency. Every relevant page clearly distinguishes confirmed catalog objects from unconfirmed candidates, explicitly labels simulated test data, and publishes negative results and sensitivity limits alongside successful detections—demonstrating to the public not only what astronomical surveys find, but how rigorous null-hypothesis testing works in practice.

11. Technical Innovations

  1. Wavelength-Matched Difference Imaging: Constructing per-pixel references exclusively from same-detector exposures within 3% in wavelength transforms SPHEREx's linear variable filter from a source of chromatic false alarms into a clean differential probe.
  2. Instantaneous Spectra from Time-Lapse Video: Clicking any pixel across arbitrary sky coordinates extracts one wavelength sample from each of hundreds of overlapping exposures, assembling a 102-band spectrum and multi-detector light curves in ≈0.5 s.
  3. Simulation-Trained Asteroid CNN with Zero Real Training Examples: Trained solely on PSF-convolved synthetic injections and real instrumental artifacts, the network achieves an AUROC of 0.987 on real asteroids in unseen fields while strictly excluding pipeline outlier flags that could leak simulation cues.
  4. Joint Parallax and Orbital-Motion Fitting: Fitting heliocentric parallax simultaneously with escape-velocity-bounded orbital motion recovers 47/48 synthetic outer Solar System bodies and measures real dwarf planets Makemake and Haumea to 0.02% and 0.66% accuracy from SPHEREx data alone.
  5. Blind-First Candidate Selection with Multi-Detector Vetting: Moving and variable star pipelines select candidates independently of external catalogs and enforce cross-detector directional/amplitude consistency to eliminate chromatic blend artifacts.
  6. Cross-Mission 10.5-Year Astrometric Baseline: Combining SPHEREx positions with CatWISE2020 (2015.4) extends proper-motion sensitivity down to 0.10–0.15″/yr, nearly an order of magnitude deeper than single-year SPHEREx data alone.
  7. Time-Propagated Catalog Overlays: Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 markers dynamically shift to the exact epoch of every survey pass, enabling immediate visual separation of known high-proper-motion stars from uncatalogued movers.
  8. Self-Hosted Grounded Bilingual AI Assistant: A fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B model paired with empirically benchmarked BGE-M3 retrieval, live site telemetry injection, and deterministic provenance badges runs entirely on local GPU hardware without external API dependencies.
  9. Pedagogical Citizen-Science Review Queue: Built-in Practice Mode hides ground-truth labels on known catalog movers until visitors cast their vote, providing immediate feedback that improves community classification quality.
  10. Zero-Downtime Automated Release Ingestion: Daily TAP polling automatically discovers and prioritizes newer SPHEREx data releases (DR over QR) without manual intervention or service interruption.

12. Design Considerations and Limitations

12.1 Engineering and Ethical Design Considerations

  • Responsiveness and Progressive Loading: Streaming frames begin playback immediately while remaining cutouts download in parallel; the initial landing page loads under 0.3 MB prior to initializing 3D assets.
  • Scientific Integrity: Zero unverified discovery claims; simulated test fields are clearly labeled; saturation and contamination flags are surfaced directly on plots; and AI responses display source citations alongside accuracy warnings.
  • Responsible Archive Stewardship: Cutouts are cached locally, parallel downloads are throttled, JPL queries are serialized with HTTP 429 backoff, and per-user rate limits protect backend resources.
  • Operational Fault Tolerance: Quick Looks run in memory-isolated systemd units, disk headroom is verified prior to weekly updates, and failed external catalog lookups cannot overwrite valid field builds.
  • User Privacy: Rate limiting uses salted IP hashes only; user queries to the AI assistant are never logged or sent to third-party services.
  • Licensing Compliance: Full-text paper indexing is restricted strictly to Creative Commons arXiv works, "Built with Llama" attribution is prominently displayed, and all astronomical archives are properly credited.

12.2 Current Limitations

  • Single-Year Proper-Motion Floor: Over a one-year SPHEREx baseline alone, stars must move at ≥0.7″/yr to show discernible motion and are recovered reliably above 2.0″/yr; slower motions rely on the CatWISE2020 cross-match, which requires source isolation (≈50% of field stars).
  • Quick-Look Artifacts Around Bright Stars: On-demand Quick Looks near bright stars can generate stationary PSF-residual false positives (explicitly labeled "Catalogue says static (likely artefact)"), and transient network timeouts during parallel cutout retrieval can occasionally omit individual frames (e.g., 36 of 290 exposures missed in the Wolf 359 run).
  • Post-DR1 Proper-Motion Recovery Drop: Following the migration from QR2 to DR1 + QR3, blind recovery on the 45 random Gaia high-proper-motion stars decreased from 25 to 19 (with median error rising from 0.27″ to 0.40″); diagnosing this regression remains active ongoing work.
  • Sparse Variable-Star Cadence: With 3–4 survey passes per field, the variable-star pipeline detects large-amplitude, long-timescale variations but cannot determine periods for short-period variables; additionally, the PSF-wing saturation threshold was calibrated on the same fields used for the Barnard's Star control.
  • Limited Real Brown-Dwarf Test Sample: Only two confirmed cold brown dwarfs (Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855-0714) were available in the benchmark fields to validate the synthetic-trained spectral classifier.
  • Quick-Look Scope: On-demand Quick Looks execute streaming playback, spectral/light-curve extraction, and proper-motion checks, whereas the CNN asteroid detector and shift-and-stack Planet X pipeline currently run only on pre-analyzed fields.
  • Injection Noise Approximations: Synthetic source injections add signal flux without per-pixel Poisson shot noise, and QR3 injections reused same-detector QR2 PSF models.
  • Compact LLM Constraints: As a 1B-parameter model, the assistant can still make reasoning errors when answering outside retrieved literature passages, and its fine-tuning dialogues were generated using an earlier English-only retrieval index.

13. Conclusion

SPHEREx Sky Change fulfills every objective and design consideration of the challenge across arbitrary sky coordinates while extending into quantitative astrophysics and citizen science. The platform streams chronological infrared imagery within a minute, extracts on-demand spectra and light curves, runs automated searches for asteroids, outer Solar System bodies, high-proper-motion stars, and variable stars, invites public candidate review, and provides a bilingual, literature-grounded AI assistant. Every module has been rigorously benchmarked against known ground-truth objects, with limitations and null results reported alongside headline successes. While the tool has not discovered a new planet, it demonstrates that SPHEREx data can measure sub-pixel asteroid astrometry, nearby stellar and brown-dwarf proper motions, and outer Solar System parallaxes—empowering anyone with a web browser to explore the evolving infrared sky.

14. AI Use

  • AI Models in the Live Product: Three machine-learning models run locally on our server infrastructure: the real/bogus CNN and the brown-dwarf spectral classifier (both trained in-house on synthetic data), and the AI assistant (Meta Llama 3.2 1B Instruct fine-tuned via LoRA, paired with BGE-M3 for retrieval). Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was used strictly offline to generate synthetic training dialogues. No external commercial AI APIs are called during live operation.
